title: QNETSIM for memory assisted design of satellite and hybrid quantum networks
authors: Seid Koudia, Francesco Vista, Heyang Peng, Ilora Maity, Intidhar Bedhief, Juan Carlos Hernandez Hernandez, Symeon Chatzinotas
abstract: Space-based quantum information networks require simulation tools that capture orbital dynamics, probabilistic quantum operations, and classical coordination. We introduce QNETSIM, a modular discrete-event simulator for the design and performance evaluation of satellite and hybrid space-ground quantum networks. The framework integrates orbital geometry, free-space optical and fiber channels, quantum memories, entanglement generation, and Bell-state measurements within a common event-driven architecture. Physical models account for optical loss, atmospheric turbulence, detector imperfections, finite memory capacity, and storage-induced decoherence. Space-time routing and segmented nesting support entanglement distribution across changing topologies, while a software-defined control plane coordinates generation, storage, and swapping. Configurable scenarios encompass onboard repeaters, satellite constellations, ground-based repeaters, and direct satellite distribution. Through explicit interfaces between physical models, network protocols, and orchestration, QNETSIM links component characteristics and operational policies to entanglement fidelity, throughput, latency, availability, and memory utilization, enabling systematic exploration of architectural and resource-management trade-offs in future space-based quantum information networks.
summary: This paper introduces QNETSIM, a sophisticated discrete-event simulator designed to model the performance of future space-based and hybrid quantum networks. It integrates complex physical effects like orbital dynamics, atmospheric loss, and memory decoherence into a unified framework. The tool allows researchers to systematically explore trade-offs between network architecture and operational resource management for quantum communication.
main_problem: The core problem is designing and evaluating complex, space-based and hybrid space-ground quantum information networks that require simulating orbital dynamics alongside quantum operations.
main_result: The proposed simulator, QNETSIM, successfully links component characteristics and operational policies to measurable network performance indicators like fidelity, throughput, and latency, enabling systematic trade-off analysis.
method: The authors developed QNETSIM, a modular discrete-event simulator, to model time-dependent quantum network processes.
model_or_system: The system models include satellite constellations, ground stations, free-space optical links, and quantum memories, all integrated into an event-driven architecture that handles orbital geometry and probabilistic quantum operations.
key_observables: Entanglement fidelity, throughput, latency, availability, and memory utilization.
important_parameters: Optical loss, atmospheric turbulence, detector imperfections, finite memory capacity, and storage-induced decoherence.
main_assumptions: The simulator explicitly models physical limitations (e.g., detector jitter, memory decoherence) rather than assuming ideal components.
figures_summary: Figures detail the layered execution and resource architecture of the simulation, showing the flow from application requests to physical outcomes across different mission scenarios.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the QNETSIM framework, details its modular components (orbital dynamics, memory, channels), presents evaluations across three distinct mission scenarios (onboard repeater, LEO constellation, ground-to-space link), and concludes by linking architectural choices to performance metrics.
why_interesting: It provides a comprehensive simulation framework that bridges quantum information theory with complex classical engineering constraints (orbital mechanics, resource management), which is crucial for realizing large-scale quantum networks.

Figure 2: Complete S1 conditional-fidelity sweep. Rows are cases A–D; the left column varies 𝑇2, and the right varies 𝜎2 𝑅. Each curve is the median of supported run-bin means over four repeats, with no temporal smoothing. Empty-support bins remain undefined. The first two rows have co-located stations, not a 1000 km separation; the lower rows have 500 km separation and an Alice-anchored pass.

Figure 3: Complete S1 rate sweep for the same 32 settings and 128 runs as Fig. 2. The ordinate is the mean recorded end-to-end delivery rate in pairs/s, obtained from 2 s bins; no rate multiplier or temporal smoothing is applied. The geometrical and observation-window definitions are given in Section 2.4.

Figure 4: Dated S1 optical conditions and delivery dynamics. (a,b) Paris and Vienna downlink budgets. (c,d) Common visibility and slant range from the geometry used for the run. (e,f) Delivery rate and conditional mean fidelity from the 2 s counting bins. Time zero is the assumed pass midpoint. Rate and fidelity use bin-end times; attached optical geometry is sampled at bin midpoints. Fidelity gaps contain no deliveries. Bank occupancy is summarized in Section 2.4.2; the component budget and illumination context are given in Section 4.7.
